section.heading: 8.1 Affine Combinations
section.paragraph: An affine combination of vectors is a special kind of linear combination. Given vectors (or “points”) $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and scalars $$c_{1},\ldots,c_{p}$$ , an affine combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$$ is a linear combination
$$c_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} \textbf{v}_{p}$$
such that the weights satisfy $$c_{1} + \cdots + c_{p} = 1$$ .﻿

note.title: ﻿Definition
note.heading: ﻿Definition
note.paragraph: The set of all affine combinations of points in a set $$S$$ is called the affine hull (or affine span) of $$S,$$ denoted by $$\text{aff} S$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: The affine hull of a single point $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ is just the set $$\left\{ \textbf{v}_{1} \right\}$$ , since it has the form $$c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1}$$ where $$c_{1} = 1$$ . The affine hull of two distinct points is often written in a special way. Suppose $$\textbf{y} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2}\textbf{v}_{2}$$ with $$c_{1} + c_{2} = 1$$ . Write $$t$$ in place of $$c_{2}$$ , so that $$c_{1} = 1 - c_{2} =$$ $$1 - t$$ . Then the affine hull of $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2}\}$$ is the set
$$\textbf{y} = \left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right) \textbf{v}_{1} + t \textbf{v}_{2} , \text{with} t \text{in} \mathbb{R}$$

This set of points includes $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ (when $$t = 0$$ ) and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ (when $$t = 1$$ ). If $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \textbf{v}_{1}$$ , then (1) again describes just one point. Otherwise, (1) describes the line through $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ . To see this, rewrite (1) in the form
$$\textbf{y} = \textbf{v}_{1} + t \left(\right. \textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1} \left.\right) = \textbf{p} + t \textbf{u} , \text{with} t \text{in} \mathbb{R}$$

where $$\textbf{p}$$ is $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{u}$$ is $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ . The set of all multiples of $$\textbf{u}$$ is $$\text{Span} \{\textbf{u}\},$$ the line through $$\textbf{u}$$ and the origin. Adding $$\textbf{p}$$ to each point on this line translates $$\text{Span} \{\textbf{u}\}$$ into the line through $$\textbf{p}$$ parallel to the line through $$\textbf{u}$$ and the origin. See Figure 1. (Compare this figure with Figure 5 in Section 1.5.)

section.paragraph: Figure 2 uses the original points $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , and displays $$\text{aff} \{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2}\}$$ as the line through $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ .﻿

image.alt: A graph shows two straight lines parallel to each other, with vectors connecting them.

section.paragraph: Notice that while the point $$\textbf{y}$$ in Figure 2 is an affine combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , the point $$\textbf{y} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ equals $$t\left( \textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1} \right)$$ , which is a linear combination (in fact, a multiple) of $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ . This relation between $$\textbf{y}$$ and $$\textbf{y} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ holds for any affine combination of points, as the following theorem shows.

note.title: Theorem 1
note.heading: Theorem 1
note.paragraph: A point $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is an affine combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ if and only if $$\textbf{y} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ is a linear combination of the translated points $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ .﻿

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: If $$\textbf{y} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ is a linear combination of $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ , there exist weights $$c_{2},\ldots,c_{p}$$ such that
$$\textbf{y} - \textbf{v}_{1} = c_{2} \left(\right. \textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1} \left.\right) + \hdots + c_{p} \left(\right. \textbf{v}_{p} - \textbf{v}_{1} \left.\right)$$
Then
and the weights in this linear combination sum to $$1$$ . So $$\textbf{y}$$ is an affine combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$$ . Conversely, suppose
$$\text{y} = \text{c} _{1} \text{v} _{1} + \text{c} _{2} \text{v} _{2} + \hdots + \text{c} _{p} \text{v} _{p}$$

where $$c_{1} + \cdots + c_{p} = 1$$ . Since $$c_{1} = 1 - c_{2} - \cdots - c_{p}$$ , equation (4) may be written as in (3), and this leads to (2), which shows that $$\textbf{y} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ is a linear combination of $$\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p} - \textbf{v}_{1}$$ .﻿

In the statement of Theorem 1, the point $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ could be replaced by any of the other points in the list $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$$ . Only the notation in the proof would change.

If possible, write $$\textbf{y}$$ as an affine combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{4}$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: While the procedure in Example 1 works for arbitrary points $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , the question can be answered more directly if the chosen points $$\textbf{v}_{i}$$ are a basis for $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . For example, let $$B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{n}\}$$ be such a basis. Then any $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a unique linear combination of $$\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{n}$$ . This combination is an affine combination of the $$\textbf{b}$$ ’s if and only if the weights sum to $$1$$ . (These weights are just the $$B \text{-coordinates}$$ of $$\textbf{y}$$ , as in Section 4.4.)

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Let $$b_{1} = \left[\right. 4 0 3 \left]\right. ,$$ $$b_{2} = \left[\right. 0 4 2 \left]\right. ,$$ $$b_{3} = \left[\right. 5 2 4 \left]\right. ,$$ $${\mathbf{p}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}},$$ and $$\mathbf{p}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ . The set $$B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},\textbf{b}_{2},\textbf{b}_{3}\}$$ is a basis for $$\mathbb{R}^{3}.$$ Determine whether the points $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ are affine combinations of the points in $$B$$ .﻿
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Find the $$B \text{-coordinates}$$ of $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ . These two calculations can be combined by row reducing the matrix $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{lllll} \mathbf{b}_{1} & \mathbf{b}_{2} & \mathbf{b}_{3} & \mathbf{p}_{1} & \mathbf{p}_{2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , with two augmented columns:
Read column $$4$$ to build $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , and read column $$5$$ to build $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ :
$$\mathbf{p}_{1} = - 2 \mathbf{b}_{1} - \mathbf{b}_{2} + 2 \mathbf{b}_{3} & \text{and} & \mathbf{p}_{2} = \frac{2}{3} \mathbf{b}_{1} + \frac{2}{3} \mathbf{b}_{2} - \frac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}_{3}$$

The sum of the weights in the linear combination for $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is $$- 1$$ , not $$1$$ , so $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is not an affine combination of the $$\textbf{b}$$ ’s. However, $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ is an affine combination of the $$\textbf{b}$$ ’s, because the sum of the weights for $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ is $$1$$ .﻿

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A set $$S$$ is affine if $$\textbf{p}$$ , $$\textbf{q} \in S$$ implies that $$(1 - t)\textbf{p} + t\textbf{q} \in S$$ for each real number $$t$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: Geometrically, a set is affine if whenever two points are in the set, the entire line through these points is in the set. (If $$S$$ contains only one point, $$\textbf{p}$$ , then the line through $$\textbf{p}$$ and $$\textbf{p}$$ is just a point, a “degenerate” line.) Algebraically, for a set $$S$$ to be affine, the definition requires that every affine combination of two points of $$S$$ belong to $$S$$ . Remarkably, this is equivalent to requiring that $$S$$ contain every affine combination of an arbitrary number of points of $$S$$ .﻿

note.title: Theorem 2
note.heading: Theorem 2
note.paragraph: A set $$S$$ is affine if and only if every affine combination of points of $$S$$ lies in $$S$$ . That is, $$S$$ is affine if and only if $$S = \text{aff} S$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: Remark: See the remark prior to Theorem 5 in Chapter 3 regarding mathematical induction.
section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Suppose that $$S$$ is affine and use induction on the number $$m$$ of points of $$S$$ occurring in an affine combination. When $$m$$ is $$1$$ or $$2$$ , an affine combination of $$m$$ points of $$S$$ lies in $$S$$ , by the definition of an affine set. Now, assume that every affine combination of $$k$$ or fewer points of $$S$$ yields a point in $$S$$ , and consider a combination of $$k + 1$$ points. Take $$\textbf{v}_{i}$$ in $$S$$ for $$i = 1,\ldots,k + 1$$ , and let $$\textbf{y} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{k}\textbf{v}_{k} + c_{k + 1}\textbf{v}_{k + 1}$$ , where $$c_{1} + \cdots + c_{k + 1} = 1$$ . Since the $$c_{i}$$ ’s sum to $$1$$ , at least one of them must not be equal to $$1$$ . By reindexing the $$\textbf{v}_{i}$$ and $$c_{i}$$ , if necessary, we may assume that $$c_{k + 1} \neq 1$$ . Let $$t = c_{1} + \cdots + c_{k}$$ . Then $$t = 1 - c_{k + 1} \neq 0$$ , and
$$\textbf{y} = ( 1 - c_{k + 1} ) \left(\frac{c_{1}}{t} \textbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + \frac{c_{k}}{t} \textbf{v}_{k}\right) + c_{k + 1} \textbf{v}_{k + 1}$$

By the induction hypothesis, the point $$\textbf{z} = (c_{1}/t)\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + (c_{k}/t)\textbf{v}_{k}$$ is in $$S$$ , since the coefficients sum to $$1$$ . Thus (6) displays $$\textbf{y}$$ as an affine combination of two points in $$S$$ , and so $$\textbf{y} \in S$$ . By the principle of induction, every affine combination of such points lies in $$S$$ . That is, $$\text{aff} S \subseteq S$$ . But the reverse inclusion, $$S \subseteq \text{aff} S$$ , always applies. Thus, when $$S = \text{aff} S$$ . Conversely, if $$S = \text{aff} S$$ , then affine combinations of two (or more) points of $$S$$ lie in $$S$$ , so $$S$$ is affine.
The next definition provides terminology for affine sets that emphasizes their close connection with subspaces of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .﻿

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A translate of a set $$S$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ by a vector $$\textbf{p}$$ is the set $$S + \textbf{p} = \left{\right. \textbf{s} + \textbf{p} : \textbf{s} \in S \left.\right}$$ .﻿2 A flat in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a translate of a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Two flats are parallel if one is a translate of the other. The dimension of a flat is the dimension of the corresponding parallel subspace. The dimension of a set $$S$$ , written as dim $$S$$ , is the dimension of the smallest flat containing $$S$$ . A line in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a flat of dimension $$1$$ . A hyperplane in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a flat of dimension $$n - 1$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: In $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , the proper subspaces3 consist of the origin $$0$$ , the set of all lines through $$0$$ , and the set of all planes through $$0$$ . Thus the proper flats in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ are points (zero-dimensional), lines (one-dimensional), and planes (two-dimensional), which may or may not pass through the origin.

The next theorem shows that these geometric descriptions of lines and planes in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ (as translates of subspaces) actually coincide with their earlier algebraic descriptions as sets of all affine combinations of two or three points, respectively.

note.title: Theorem 3
note.heading: Theorem 3
note.paragraph: A nonempty set $$S$$ is affine if and only if it is a flat.

section.paragraph: Remark: Notice the key role that definitions play in this proof. For example, the first part assumes that $$S$$ is affine and seeks to show that $$S$$ is a flat. By definition, a flat is a translate of a subspace. By choosing $$\textbf{p}$$ in $$S$$ and defining $$W = S + \left( - \textbf{p} \right)$$ , the set $$S$$ is translated to the origin and $$S = W + \textbf{p}$$ . It remains to show that $$W$$ is a subspace, for then $$S$$ will be a translate of a subspace and hence a flat.
section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Suppose that $$S$$ is affine. Let $$\textbf{p}$$ be any fixed point in $$S$$ and let
$$W = S + \left(\right. - \textbf{p} \left.\right) , \text{so that} S = W + \textbf{p}$$

To show that $$S$$ is a flat, it suffices to show that $$W$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Since $$\textbf{p}$$ is in $$S$$ , the zero vector is in $$W$$ . To show that $$W$$ is closed under sums and scalar multiples, it suffices to show that if $$\textbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{u}_{2}$$ are elements of $$W$$ , then $$\textbf{u}_{1} + t\textbf{u}_{2}$$ is in $$W$$ for every real $$t$$ . That is, we want to show that $$\textbf{u}_{1} + t\textbf{u}_{2}$$ is in $$S + \left( - \textbf{p} \right)$$ . Since $$\textbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{u}_{2}$$ are in $$W$$ , there exist $$\textbf{s}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{s}_{2}$$ in $$S$$ such that
$$\textbf{u}_{1} = \textbf{s}_{1} - \textbf{p} \text{and} \textbf{u}_{2} = \textbf{s}_{2} - \textbf{p}$$
It follows that
$$\mathbf{u}_{1} + t \mathbf{u}_{2} & = & \mathbf{s}_{1} - \mathbf{p} + t \left(\right. \mathbf{s}_{2} - \mathbf{p} \left.\right) & = & \mathbf{s}_{1} + t \mathbf{s}_{2} - t \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}$$

Regrouping the first three terms, we find that $$\textbf{s}_{1} + t\textbf{s}_{2} - t\textbf{p}$$ is in $$S$$ since the coefficients sum to $$1$$ and $$S$$ is affine. (See Theorem 2.) So $$\textbf{u}_{1} + t\textbf{u}_{2}$$ is in $$S - \textbf{p} = W$$ . This shows that $$W$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Thus $$S$$ is a flat, because $$S = W + \textbf{p}$$ .﻿

Conversely, suppose that $$S$$ is a flat. That is, $$S = W + \textbf{p}$$ for some $$\textbf{p}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and some subspace $$W$$ . To show that $$S$$ is affine, it suffices to show that for any pair $$\textbf{s}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{s}_{2}$$ of points in $$S$$ , the line through $$\textbf{s}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{s}_{2}$$ lies in $$S$$ . By the definition of $$W$$ , there exist $$\textbf{u}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{u}_{2}$$ in $$W$$ such that
$$\textbf{s}_{1} = \textbf{u}_{1} + \textbf{p} \text{and} \textbf{s}_{2} = \textbf{u}_{2} + \textbf{p}$$
So, for each real $$t$$ we have

$$\left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right) \mathbf{s}_{1} + t \mathbf{s}_{2} & = & \left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right) \left(\right. \mathbf{u}_{1} + \mathbf{p} \left.\right) + t \left(\right. \mathbf{u}_{2} + \mathbf{p} \left.\right) & = & \left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right) \mathbf{u}_{1} + \left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right) \mathbf{p} + t \mathbf{u}_{2} + t \mathbf{p} & = & \left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right) \mathbf{u}_{1} + t \mathbf{u}_{2} + \mathbf{p}$$
Since $$W$$ is a subspace, $$(1 - t)\textbf{u}_{1} + t\textbf{u}_{2}$$ is in $$W$$ and so $$(1 - t)\textbf{s}_{1} + t\textbf{s}_{2}$$ is in $$W + \textbf{p} = S$$ . Thus, $$S$$ is affine.

Theorem 3 provides a geometric way to view the affine hull of a set: it is the flat that consists of all the affine combinations of points in the set. For instance, Figure 3 shows the points studied in Example 2. Although the set of all linear combinations of $$\textbf{b}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{b}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{b}_{3}$$ is all of $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , the set of all affine combinations is only the plane through $$\textbf{b}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{b}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{b}_{3}$$ . Note that $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ (from Example 2) is in the plane through $$\textbf{b}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{b}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{b}_{3}$$ , while $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is not in that plane. Also, see Exercise 22.

section.paragraph: The next example takes a fresh look at a familiar set—the set of all solutions of a system $$A \textbf{x} = \textbf{b} .$$

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Suppose that the solutions of an equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ are all of the form $$\textbf{x} = x_{3}\textbf{u} + \textbf{p}$$ , where $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ {- 3} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\mathbf{p} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ {- 3} \end{bmatrix}$$ , Recall from Section 1.5 that this set is parallel to the solution set of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ , which consists of all points of the form $$x_{3}\textbf{u}$$ . Find points $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ such that the solution set of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ is $$\text{aff} \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2} \right\}$$ .﻿
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The solution set is a line through $$\textbf{p}$$ in the direction of $$\textbf{u}$$ , as in Figure 1. Since $$\text{aff} \{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2}\}$$ is a line through $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , identify two points on the line $$\textbf{x} = x_{3}\textbf{u} + \textbf{p}$$ . Two simple choices appear when $$x_{3} = 0$$ and $$x_{3} = 1$$ . That is, take $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \textbf{p}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \textbf{u} + \textbf{p}$$ , so that
$$v_{2} = u + p = \left[\right. 2 - 3 1 \left]\right. + \left[\right. 4 0 - 3 \left]\right. = \left[\right. 6 - 3 - 2 \left]\right.$$
In this case, the solution set is described as the set of all affine combinations of the form
$$x = \left(\right. 1 - x_{3} \left.\right) \left[\right. 4 0 - 3 \left]\right. + x_{3} \left[\right. 6 - 3 - 2 \left]\right.$$

section.paragraph: Earlier, Theorem 1 displayed an important connection between affine combinations and linear combinations. The next theorem provides another view of affine combinations, which for $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ and $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ is closely connected to applications in computer graphics, discussed in the next section (and in Section 2.7).

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: For $$\textbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , the standard homogeneous form of $$\textbf{v}$$ is the point $$\overset{}{\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}$$ .﻿

note.title: Theorem 4
note.heading: Theorem 4
note.paragraph: A point $$\textbf{y}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is an affine combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ if and only if the homogeneous form of $$\textbf{y}$$ is in $$\text{Span\{} {\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}}_{1},\ldots,{\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}}_{p} \text{\}}$$ . In fact, $$\textbf{y} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{p}\textbf{v}_{p}$$ , with $$c_{1} + \cdots + c_{p} = 1$$ , if and only if $$\overset{\sim}{\textbf{y}} = c_{1}{\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}}_{1} + \cdots + c_{p}{\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}}_{p}$$ .﻿

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: A point $$\textbf{y}$$ is in $$\text{aff} \{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\}$$ if and only if there exist weights $$c_{1},\ldots,c_{p}$$ such that

$$\left[\right. \textbf{y} 1 \left]\right. = c_{1} \left[\right. \textbf{v}_{1} 1 \left]\right. + c_{2} \left[\right. \textbf{v}_{2} 1 \left]\right. + \hdots + c_{p} \left[\right. \textbf{v}_{p} 1 \left]\right.$$
This happens if and only if $$\widetilde{\textbf{y}}$$ is in $$\text{Span\{} {\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}}_{1},{\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}}_{2},\ldots,{\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}}_{p} \text{\}}$$ .﻿

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Let $$\mathbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{3} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ , and $$\mathbf{p} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 3 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Use Theorem 4 to write $$\textbf{p}$$ as an affine combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ , if possible.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Row reduce the augmented matrix for the equation
$$x_{1} \left(\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}\right)_{1} + x_{2} \left(\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}\right)_{2} + x_{3} \left(\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}\right)_{3} = \overset{\sim}{\textbf{p}}$$

To simplify the arithmetic, move the fourth row of 1’s to the top (equivalent to three row interchanges). After this, the number of arithmetic operations here is basically the same as the number needed for the method using Theorem 1.

$$\begin{matrix}\left[\right. \begin{matrix}\left(\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}\right)_{1} & \left(\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}\right)_{2} & \left(\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}\right)_{3} & \overset{\sim}{p}\end{matrix} \left]\right. ∼ & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 & 7 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. ∼ & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & - 2 & - 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 6 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & - 1\end{matrix} \left]\right.\end{matrix} ∼ \hdots ∼ \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 1.5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & - 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & .5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$

By Theorem 4, $$1.5\textbf{v}_{1} - \textbf{v}_{2} + .5\textbf{v}_{3} = \textbf{p}$$ . See Figure 4, which shows the plane that contains $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}$$ (together with points on the coordinate axes).
